**Observations:**

- Field-level view of soybean plants
- Several plants in the center/foreground appear stunted, with yellowing and wilting compared to healthy green plants surrounding them
- Affected plants show a distinct patch of decline — shorter, more open canopy, lighter green to yellowish coloration
- No obvious foliar lesions visible at this scale
- Sandy/dry soil visible, consistent with root/stem rot conditions
- The patchy, localized decline pattern with stunted plants is characteristic of a soilborne pathogen

**Reasoning:**

The image shows a field patch with stunted, yellowing soybean plants amid otherwise healthy ones. This patchy field decline with no visible leaf lesions, combined with what appears to be wilting/stunting, points toward a soilborne disease. Sudden death syndrome (SDS) and Phytophthora both cause this kind of field patchiness, but:

- SDS typically shows interveinal chlorosis/necrosis on leaves (not clearly visible here but scale is large)
- Phytophthora causes damping-off and root/stem rot with wilting and stunting in patches, especially in wet or compacted soils
- The sandy dry soil and general plant collapse/stunting with no distinct leaf spotting is also consistent with Charcoal Rot or Sudden Death Syndrome

The patchy field decline with stunted, yellowing plants (some appearing to have died or collapsed) most strongly resembles **Sudden_death_syndrome**, which causes premature death in patches with foliar symptoms developing from root infection. The overall plant architecture (open, sparse canopy in the affected zone) and the field-level patchiness are classic SDS presentation.
